AGENTIC SDLC | PREMIUM EDITION V0.6

How to read this guide
The cover and visual mind map serve as the entry point and GPS for the journey. This page translates that map into an operational reading path: from traditional SDLC to agent-based execution.

The central idea
AI can speed up the mechanic. Agentic Software Development starts to require us to redesign the pit stop. The gains come not just from the model, but from the engineering system around it.

From SDLC to agentic execution
SDLC | AI-assisted | Agentic execution
Need → Spec | Prompt + Context | Agent Loop
Architecture | Codebase + AGENTS.md | Harness + Skills + Tools
Build / Test | Tests + Evals | Quality Gates + Policy
Release / Operate | CI/CD + Observability | Identity + Sandbox + Audit
Learn | Metrics + Feedback | Autonomy + Platform + Scale

How to think about the system
Intent defines what we want. Context makes the problem understandable. The agent loop decides and acts. Skills teach procedures. Tools enable action. The harness connects everything to boundaries, feedback and validation. Quality gates and policy keep authority outside the model.

AGENTIC SDLC | PREMIUM EDITION V0.6

Before you begin: why this guide exists
This guide was designed for people who are just getting started with AI-assisted and Agentic Software Development but need to develop a production engineering perspective, not merely learn how to use a code generation tool.

The question guiding this material is simple: what needs to change in the engineering system when an agent moves beyond suggesting code and starts executing work?

The focus is therefore not on the model in isolation. We will study SDLC, intent, context, codebase, instructions, harness, skills, tools, tests, quality gates, sandbox, identity, CI/CD, observability, autonomy, metrics and operations. The same reasoning will be connected to a Java 25 + Spring Boot lab to turn concepts into concrete decisions.

How to study
Do not try to memorize the alphabet soup. For each concept, answer: what problem existed? Why did this become relevant? What is it? How does it work? How does it connect to everything else? How would I prove it in the lab?

0. Before agents: understand the SDLC
SDLC stands for Software Development Life Cycle: the set of activities that turns a need into operational software that delivers results. The name sounds bureaucratic, but the concept is simple: software does not begin with a commit. Before that come discovery, problem definition, requirements and architecture; afterward come implementation, validation, release, operations and learning.

The exact form varies between companies, but a useful map is:
Need / Idea → Discovery → Requirements / Specs → Architecture → Build → Test → Release → Operate → Observe → Learn

DevOps did not eliminate the SDLC; it brought development and operations closer together, automated feedback and reduced handoffs. CI/CD made build, testing and delivery more repeatable. SRE brought reliability and SLOs into the conversation. Platform Engineering reduced cognitive load by turning good practices into platforms and paved roads.

AI now adds a new actor to the system. It first arrived as an assistant: autocomplete, chat, explanations and test generation. With agents, part of the execution can be delegated. This changes the question from “How does the developer use AI?” to “How does the system enable an agent to work with safety, context and evidence?”

Food for thought
If generating code has become cheap, the bottleneck does not disappear: it moves. A stage that is 10x faster may simply create a queue at the next stage. The goal remains to reduce the time between a need and value delivered safely.

AGENTIC SDLC | PREMIUM EDITION V0.6

1. From assistive AI to Agentic SDLC

Context before the concept
This chapter builds on the SDLC presented in the introduction. Agentic SDLC does not replace software engineering: it changes who executes certain stages and what controls must surround that execution.

Agentic SDLC SDLC
“Agentic SDLC” is an emerging label for engineering systems in which agents execute significant parts of the development lifecycle. There is no single normative definition. The most important distinction is operational: in AI-assisted development, the human continues to execute the workflow and AI assists; in agentic work, the system delegates objectives and the agent chooses steps, uses tools, observes results and iterates within boundaries.

A workflow is not the same as an agent
Anthropic uses a useful distinction: workflows orchestrate models and tools through predefined paths; agents allow the model to dynamically direct the process and tool selection. In practice, good systems combine both: determinism where the path must be controlled and agentic behavior where adaptation adds value.

What changes in the engineer's role
When execution is partially delegated, human work shifts toward defining intent, designing constraints, architecture, context, quality gates, observability and evaluating outcomes. OpenAI's Harness Engineering case is evidence of a real implementation, not a universal standard.

Technology-agnostic example: task reminder
A generic task management service receives a new capability: sending a reminder 24 hours before the due date. The rule must respect the user's time zone and preferences, prevent duplicate reminders, tolerate transient failures from the notification provider and produce enough telemetry to prove whether the reminder was delivered. In assistive mode, AI suggests the implementation. In agentic mode, it receives the spec, explores the repository, makes changes, runs tests, fixes failures and prepares the change for review.
